    "response": {
      "output": "Quicksort has an average-case time complexity of O(n log n) and a worst-case of O(n²), which occurs when the pivot selection is poor (e.g. already sorted input with first-element pivot). Mergesort guarantees O(n log n) in all cases — best, average, and worst — because it always divides the array in half. However, mergesort requires O(n) auxiliary space for the merge step, while quicksort operates in-place with O(log n) stack space on average. Quicksort is generally preferred for in-memory sorting due to better cache locality and lower constant factors, while mergesort is preferred for linked lists (no random access needed) and external sorting (sequential access patterns). In practice, many libraries use hybrid approaches like Timsort (merge + insertion sort) or introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback)."
    }
  },
  "retrieval_context": {
    "output": "Quicksort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm with average time complexity O(n log n) and worst-case O(n²). The worst case arises from consistently choosing the smallest or largest element as pivot. Mergesort is also comparison-based with guaranteed O(n log n) time complexity in all cases. Mergesort requires O(n) additional memory for merging, whereas quicksort is an in-place algorithm requiring O(log n) auxiliary space on average. Quicksort generally has better cache performance due to sequential memory access patterns within partitions. Mergesort is stable and preferred for linked lists and external sorting. Many modern implementations use hybrid algorithms: Python uses Timsort (mergesort + insertion sort), and C++ STL typically uses introsort (quicksort + heapsort)."
